purpose: Adaptive business assessment questions that identify business needs independent of AI. Questions are organized by category and subcategory so a program can ask initial categorization questions, then trigger deeper follow-up questions and map the results to businessresults.json.

categories.label: Customer Interaction
categories.description: Questions about how reliably the business responds to customers, follows through, maintains visibility, and handles load.

initial_question.text: How consistently does the business respond to customer inquiries or requests in a timely way?

options.text: Responses are often missed or highly inconsistent.
Responses usually happen, but timing varies a lot.
Responses are generally timely, though lapses still occur.
Responses are timely, predictable, and clearly owned.

0.text: When responses are missed, what is the most common reason?

options.text: No one clearly owns the response.
People are too busy and the work gets lost.
Information is scattered and hard to act on.
We do not really have a response process.
It depends on who notices the issue first.
Busy periods create delays.
Handoffs between people slow us down.
We have a pattern, but it is not always followed.

2.text: What most often causes the remaining response lapses?

options.text: Workload spikes.
Backup ownership is unclear.
Some requests are harder to route than others.
Lapses are rare and usually corrected quickly.

initial_question.text: How reliably are customer inquiries, leads, or open issues followed through to completion?

options.text: Items are frequently forgotten or dropped.
Some follow-up happens, but many items still fall through the cracks.
Most important items receive follow-up, though gaps still occur.
Follow-up is systematic and rarely missed.

0.text: How are open customer commitments usually tracked today?

options.text: Mostly memory or inboxes.
Paper notes or personal reminders.
A loose spreadsheet or list that is not maintained consistently.
There is no real tracking method.

1.text: Why do follow-ups still get missed?

options.text: Ownership is unclear.
Open items are not visible enough.
People know what to do, but routine slips under pressure.
We revisit items, but not in a disciplined way.

2.text: What best describes the remaining follow-up gaps?

options.text: They happen mainly during busy periods.
They occur mostly during handoffs.
They are uncommon and visible when they happen.
They are tied to a few types of requests.

initial_question.text: How easy is it to see a customer's status, history, and next steps without having to reconstruct the situation?

options.text: It is very difficult; information is scattered or missing.
Some information exists, but it is fragmented and hard to trust.
We can usually determine the situation, though it takes some effort.
Customer status and next steps are clear and accessible.

0.text: Where does customer information usually live?

options.text: Mostly in people's memory.
In separate inboxes or personal files.
Across disconnected tools.
In conversations more than in records.
Information is incomplete.
Information exists but is not current.
People track things differently.
We can find it, but it takes too much effort.

initial_question.text: What happens to customer service and follow-through when demand increases?

options.text: Service breaks down quickly.
We manage normal demand, but busy periods create visible strain.
We can handle moderate increases, though strain still appears.
Service quality remains stable even when demand rises.

0.text: What usually breaks first when volume rises?

options.text: Response times.
Follow-up and tracking.
Internal coordination.
Quality becomes inconsistent everywhere.

1.text: Why does strain show up during busier periods?

options.text: We do not have enough backup ownership.
Processes work only at normal volume.
A few people carry too much of the load.
We recover, but only with extra effort.

categories.label: Marketing
categories.description: Questions about creating demand, communicating value, measuring effectiveness, and converting interest into customers.

initial_question.text: How intentionally does the business create new customer interest?

options.text: New business mostly comes by chance, referrals, or existing relationships.
We market occasionally, usually when demand slows down.
We market regularly, though results are not yet very predictable.
We create demand through an intentional, repeatable approach.

0.text: What best describes current growth sources?

options.text: Mostly referrals.
Mostly repeat customers.
Mostly word of mouth with little deliberate outreach.
We do not really have a growth system.
It gets deprioritized when operations get busy.
No one clearly owns it.
We are unsure what works.
We do some useful things, but not on a schedule.

2.text: What is keeping demand generation from being more predictable?

options.text: Channel performance varies too much.
Messaging is not yet sharp enough.
We need better measurement and refinement.
We are close; the system mostly works.

initial_question.text: How clearly does the business explain what it does, who it serves, and why it matters?

options.text: Our message is unclear, inconsistent, or too generic.
We can explain it, but the message shifts too much.
Our message is reasonably clear, though it still needs refinement.
Our value proposition is clear, focused, and consistently communicated.

0.text: What is the biggest messaging problem today?

options.text: We are not clear about our differentiators.
We try to say too many things at once.
Different people describe us differently.
We are not sure who our message is really for.

1.text: Where does messaging vary the most?

options.text: Between people.
Across channels.
Between offers or services.
The core message is there, but not applied consistently.

initial_question.text: How well does the business understand what marketing efforts are actually producing results?

options.text: We do not really know what is working.
We notice some signals, but they are not reliable enough to guide decisions.
We track useful indicators, though we do not always act on them consistently.
We measure performance and use it to improve outcomes.

0.text: What best describes current marketing feedback?

options.text: Mostly intuition.
Anecdotal feedback from customers.
Occasional signals, but not tracked.
Very little useful feedback exists.

1.text: Why does feedback not drive decisions more effectively?

options.text: We do not review it consistently.
The data is incomplete.
We are unsure how to interpret what we see.
Some useful signals exist, but the review habit is weak.

initial_question.text: How effectively does the business turn customer interest into actual business?

options.text: A lot of interest drops off before becoming revenue.
Some leads convert, but the process is uneven.
We convert a reasonable share of opportunities, though inefficiencies remain.
We reliably convert qualified interest into customers.

0.text: Where does the biggest drop-off usually occur?

options.text: After inquiry, before follow-up.
After initial conversation, before decision.
Because our message does not create enough confidence.
Because there is no disciplined conversion path.
Variation in follow-up.
Variation in who handles the lead.
Weak visibility into where prospects drop off.
We convert reasonably well, just not predictably.

categories.label: Operations
categories.description: Questions about how clearly work is defined, how consistently it is executed, how much waste is created through rework, and how well the business handles growth.

initial_question.text: How clearly is core work defined in the business?

options.text: Work is mostly improvised.
Some routines exist, but they are informal and inconsistent.
Core processes are generally understood, though variation still occurs.
Core work is performed through clear, stable, repeatable processes.

0.text: What best describes how work gets done today?

options.text: Each person handles it differently.
People mostly rely on experience and judgment.
There is little shared process clarity.
Important work is not clearly defined.
They are not documented or reinforced.
Different people interpret them differently.
They work in some cases, but not others.
We have useful habits, but not a strong operating routine.

initial_question.text: How consistent are outcomes when the business performs the same kind of work?

options.text: Outcomes vary a lot depending on who does the work or what else is going on.
Some consistency exists, but variation is still common.
Most work follows a consistent pattern, with occasional deviation.
Execution is reliable and predictable across people and circumstances.

initial_question.text: How much time does the business spend fixing mistakes, redoing work, or correcting avoidable problems?

options.text: A great deal; rework is frequent and disruptive.
Issues happen regularly and create ongoing drag.
Errors still occur, but they are manageable.
Errors are minimized and resolved quickly.

initial_question.text: How well can the business handle growth or increased workload without breakdown?

options.text: The business breaks down under increased demand.
We can absorb some growth, but strain appears quickly.
We can handle moderate growth, though strain is still visible.
We scale smoothly without major decline in quality or coordination.

categories.label: Time Usage
categories.description: Questions about how effectively the business converts effort into meaningful progress through planning, focus, delegation, and decision distribution.

initial_question.text: How much of the business's time is spent reacting to immediate issues instead of advancing planned priorities?

options.text: Most time is reactive.
Reactive work still dominates, though some planning occurs.
There is a workable balance between reactive and planned work.
Time is primarily directed toward planned priorities.

initial_question.text: How well does the business protect uninterrupted time for important work?

options.text: Focused work is rare because interruptions are constant.
Focused work happens occasionally, but it is easily disrupted.
We can usually protect some important work time, though interruptions still occur.
Important work is generally protected from disruption.

initial_question.text: How well is work distributed across the business rather than concentrated in a few people?

options.text: Work is concentrated in a few people.
Some delegation exists, but key people are still overloaded.
Work is reasonably distributed, though a few dependencies remain.
Work and responsibility are well distributed.

initial_question.text: How much routine decision-making is still concentrated in leadership or a few central people?

options.text: Leadership is required for a large share of normal decisions.
Some decisions are delegated, but leadership is still pulled into too much.
Many routine decisions are handled appropriately, though bottlenecks remain.
Decision-making is distributed at the appropriate level.
